catalog_quote: There are two tones in the language, H and L, and contrary to suggestions by Driberg or Tucker and Bryan, there is nothing which could be called stress. It is a general characteristic of the phonology and phonetics of the language that occurrence of H tone is rather restricted, in that an H tone generally occurs only once in a word, if at all. Generally, the H tone occurs only on one of the last three syllables of the word. Multiple adjacent H tones may occasionally be found, as in doyólééc "child", but otherwise two H tones are not found in a word, and two nonadjacent H tones are never found in a word (except by applying a tone sandhi rule) ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Didinga is a two-tone language (H, L); Odden, the most authoritative phonological description, explicitly denies the existence of word stress, rejecting the stress marks of Driberg 1931 and Tucker & Bryan 1966. The older sources agree that most words show no audible stress: Driberg 1931 (n. 1 to the orthography key) marks an acute-accent 'word-stress, which is liable to be changed by inflection' on some words but says 'in a large number of words no stress is observable, all the syllables being given an equal value'; Rosato 1980 ('Notes', c) says 'Normally all syllables have the same stress in D. There are a few exceptions' and gives one minimal pair (kagà 'I know' vs kaga adv.), which in Odden's analysis is a tonal difference.
new_statements.exceptions: Driberg 1931: some words carry an acute-accent stress that shifts under inflection; Rosato 1980: 'a few exceptions', one example kagà vs kaga. Odden 1983 treats all such prominence as H vs L tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Driberg speaks of 'word-stress'); statements are about citation forms in grammar sketches, no instrumental data. Odden's discussion continues with the restricted distribution of H tone; de Jong 2004 (open, downloaded) describes only two level tones with low lexical but important grammatical functional load and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Didinga proper (didi1258, Chukudum/Lowudo area of the Didinga Hills). Rosato's 'D.' = Didinga. The Goedemans & van der Hulst 2010 stress entry found in passing is for Murle (murl1244), the sister language, not Didinga. de Jong 2004 also compares Murle and Tennet graphemes but its phonology is Didinga.

sources.note: Silent on stress. Section 8 'Tone' (p. 159): 'Didinga has two level tones, high and low. Falling and rising tones normally occur on long vowels and are interpreted as sequences of high-low and low-high. The functional load of lexical tone is low.' Grammatical tone (nominative vs. object, verb person/aspect) is described; no mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text).
